tagline.text: Baguio's military academy that trains Philippine officers

location.label: Location
location.text: Loakan Road, Baguio (Fort Gen. Gregorio H. del Pilar)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (check locally which weekdays and weekends have cadet training)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱150~600 (per person, covering transport, museum and snacks)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), then overland

children.text: The Philippine Military Academy (PMA) is the officer-training institution of the Armed Forces of the Philippines, on a campus of about 373 hectares in Loakan, south of Baguio. Visitors can see cadet drills, a museum and displays of retired tanks and aircraft. Access rules change from time to time, so check before you visit.

The Philippine Military Academy (PMA) is at Fort Gen. Gregorio H. del Pilar in the Loakan area, about 10 kilometers south of downtown Baguio. According to Wikipedia, the campus covers about 373 hectares, and the academy, modeled on the United States Military Academy and established under the National Defense Act of 1935, is the leading officer-training institution of the Armed Forces of the Philippines. It is sometimes compared to West Point. The equestrian statue near the entrance depicts General Gregorio del Pilar, the hero of the Battle of Tirad Pass, for whom the fort is named. According to PMA's own introduction, visitors can explore the campus and watch cadets drill, and the museum lets you see vintage tanks and weapons. Wikipedia also notes that the campus has the Air Power Park, which displays retired aircraft.

Its history begins on October 25, 1898, with the Academia Militar, established in Malolos, Bulacan, by decree of President Aguinaldo. The school closed in January 1899 when war with the Americans broke out. On February 17, 1905, a Philippine Constabulary Officers' School opened in Intramuros, Manila, and on September 1, 1908 it moved to Baguio and continued at Camp Henry Allen. It was renamed the Philippine Constabulary Academy in 1928, and the present PMA came into being under the National Defense Act of 1935. Training was interrupted by World War II and resumed on May 5, 1947 at Camp Henry T. Allen, after which the academy moved to its present site. Melchor Hall, the central building of the campus, was completed in 1949. Women have been admitted as cadets since 1993.

Cadets undergo four years of demanding education and training for their degree and commission. About 400 people enter each June, begin with Reception Ceremonies on June 1 and go through eight weeks of summer training, and graduation and commissioning take place in May. Cadets are said to live by an honor code: cadets do not lie, cheat or steal, nor tolerate among them those who do. What visitors see here is not simply a tourist attraction but the daily life of such an institution, so what you can see depends on the training and event schedule. In a 2011 news report, the superintendent at the time said, "PMA is always open to the public." However, that summer the cadets were dispersed to training areas, so weekend parades and silent drills were less frequent and visitors had fewer chances to see cadets in action. In other words, what you can see changes with the training schedule.

This guide is for travelers who plan a day in Baguio and are interested in military history or unusual places. Walking among the museum, the display areas, the equestrian statue and plaza, and the training fields, two or three hours pass quickly. Because it is a military installation, entry procedures, photography rules, and museum hours and fees vary over time, so it is safest to check with the official contacts before visiting. Information differs across sources in many places, so give priority to on-site notices and staff instructions.
Past the gate stands an equestrian statue of General Gregorio del Pilar, the hero of Tirad Pass. He is the person for whom the fort is named, and it is the first monument you see.

It exhibits the history of PMA, its founders, key figures and memorabilia. Reports mention uniforms from 1908 to the present, a painting of the Battle of Tirad Pass, a recreated cadet room and weapons displays. Fees and hours must be confirmed locally. A souvenir shop is described as being near the museum.

An outdoor area displaying retired weapons and vehicles such as 105mm howitzers, a Sherman tank, a self-propelled howitzer and a mountain gun. It is described as possible to climb on the tanks. Aircraft displays such as an old Navy helicopter can also be seen.
The field where cadet training and parades are held. You can enjoy a view from the Tirso G. Fajardo Memorial Grandstand, and there is said to be a sign with the motto "Courage, Integrity, Loyalty."
An exhibition area for retired Air Force aircraft that opened on February 18, 2022. Types such as the Northrop F-5, Vought F-8 Crusader and Bell UH-1 Iroquois are said to be on display.

blocks.title: Dimalupig Park and the view deck

children.text: A park with information explaining the cadet class years (First Class to Fourth Class), a tree house and a view deck. It is a nice place to rest, and the curving paths are described as good for photos.

Facilities and monuments such as Saint Ignatius Chapel, the Our Lady of Fatima Grotto and Cavaliers Park (a Philippine-American memorial project) are found around the campus. The sundial in front of Melchor Hall and the headquarters building is also worth a look.

items.title: Half-day PMA route
items.subtitle: From the main gate to the museum

children.text: Take a jeepney or taxi from downtown Baguio toward Loakan and arrive at the Fort del Pilar main gate. Check the entry instructions and see the equestrian statue near the gate first.
Go deeper into the campus by vehicle or on foot and look at Melchor Hall, the headquarters and the sundial.
Visit the PMA Museum. Confirm hours and fees locally.
At Relics Point, look around the displays of retired tanks, cannons and helicopters.
If cadets are training at Borromeo Field and the grandstand, watch from a distance. Ask the staff first whether photography is allowed.
Browse snacks and military souvenirs at the campus canteen or gift shop, then return to downtown.
On days without cadet training you will mostly see the museum and displays. Adjust the plan to the situation on site.
If it is a Sunday morning, leave downtown early. Some sources mention a cadet parade at 9 a.m. on Sundays, but it varies by season, so confirm in advance.
Head toward Borromeo Field and watch the training or ceremony preparations.
After the parade ends, look around the museum and display areas.
Eat lunch on campus or back downtown.
Parades and drills are said to be held often on weekends, but the schedule is not guaranteed. Ask PMA for exact dates.
A long-distance bus from Manila to Baguio takes about
5–6 hours
depending on traffic. Check the bus company's announcements for departure terminals and fares.
By private or rental car, the route goes via NLEX, SCTEX and TPLEX and takes around
4 hours
After arriving in Baguio, head toward Loakan.
Getting from Manila to Baguio overland is the usual choice. Check the bus company's announcements for the latest operating information.
Take a PMA/Loakan jeepney from the stop near Burnham Park. One blog gives about
one way and at least
25 minutes
when traffic is light.
Confirm with the driver whether the jeepney goes inside PMA. Some drop passengers in front of the main gate.
The distance from the main gate to the center of the campus is considerable, so allow for the walking time.
A taxi or Grab from downtown takes around
20–30 minutes
, and the fare varies with traffic. Asking the driver to wait for a round trip is convenient.
By car, follow Loakan Road, pass the fork toward Loakan Airport and keep straight; the Fort del Pilar main gate is on the right. It is about
10 km
from Burnham Park.
Many Baguio city tour packages include PMA.

There are many outdoor facilities and monuments, so the weather matters. Baguio is cool all year, but frequent rain in the wet season means you will mostly see the museum and indoor displays. The dry season from November to May is best for walking. Training schedules change with the season, so what there is to see can differ from year to year even in the same month.

The atmosphere at PMA changes a lot with the event calendar. Graduation and commissioning take place in May, and in early June there are the reception of new cadets and summer training. February is described as having an alumni homecoming and celebrations. Entry may be restricted at these times, so inquire before visiting.

There is no lodging for travelers inside PMA, so most visitors stay in downtown Baguio and come for the day. Around Burnham Park and Session Road there are many hotels, guesthouses and Korean-run guesthouses, which makes getting around easy. There is some lodging on the Loakan side, but the choice is wider downtown.

The campus is described as having a canteen and gift shop where you can get snacks and drinks. It is easier to return downtown for meals, and Baguio has quite a few Korean restaurants. In military areas there may be rules about eating, so follow the staff's instructions.
After seeing PMA, the usual plan is to eat in the nearby Loakan area or back downtown. Restaurant names in this area change often, so check recent reviews.
Before you go, check with PMA's official contacts whether it is open and what procedures apply. The phone numbers (074) 447-3690 and (074) 442-5520 are given.
Reports say cadet drills and parades are held on weekends, but they can be rare depending on the season, so enjoy them as a bonus rather than expecting them.
When taking a jeepney, ask the driver first whether it goes inside PMA.
The museum, Relics Point and Borromeo Field are some distance from the main gate, so wear comfortable shoes if you plan to walk.
This is a military installation, so ask staff first where photography is allowed and do not photograph cadets without permission.
Combining it with Wright Park and Camp John Hay makes a half-day to full-day route.
PMA is often included in Baguio city tour packages, so if getting around on your own is a burden, taking a tour is another option.
Dress neatly, and check detailed rules such as bag restrictions with the staff at the entrance.

PMA is a military educational institution. Entry procedures and photography rules change from time to time, and visits may be restricted depending on the security situation, so be sure to check before you go.
Entry rules and museum fees and hours differ between sources and need to be confirmed locally.
Entry for outsiders may be restricted during graduation and commissioning and other major events.
Photography in military installations may be allowed only in designated areas, so follow the staff's instructions.
The campus is large, and if the jeepney does not go inside, the walking distance becomes long.
There is no guarantee you will see cadets and training, so think of watching drills as a bonus.
An area of pine forest and former resort buildings, easy to combine with PMA on a day trip near downtown.
A park near downtown and the plaza in front of the presidential residence, which can be added to a half-day route.
From PMA to the city center is about
10 km
. It is best to choose lodging and restaurants downtown.
A park in the center of downtown with a jeepney stop. It is described as the starting point for taking a PMA jeepney.
